items.title: Compilers for LLM Graphs
items.abstract:
Compilers for LLM Graphs was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on developer platforms, observability, and workflow automation around LLM applications. The project referenced by this session is apache/tvm. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source tvm project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The session surveys the toolchain around modern model applications: tracing, prompt management, evals, deployment, and incident response.

Prompt versioning is treated like code versioning, with review, rollback, and environment promotion rules that prevent accidental regressions.

The talk demonstrates a local-first workflow where developers can replay a failing request with the exact model, prompt, and tool state that produced it.

Compiler and runtime approaches are compared for graph-structured applications, including scheduling, caching, and partial re-execution.

Integration patterns are shown for CI pipelines that block releases when evaluation thresholds regress.

The closing discussion focuses on developer experience for non-specialists who build with natural-language interfaces.

Method and measurement. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic.

Takeaways. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check.

Session context. The session is part of a longer track on building dependable model applications for internal and external users. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. The speaker contrasted research prototypes with systems that must run unattended overnight and recover from partial failures.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

items.abstract:
Efficient Attention with IO Awareness was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The session contrasts speculative decoding, lookahead decoding, and draft-model approaches, noting that acceptance rates are workload dependent.

The speaker frames serving as a scheduling problem: requests, KV cache blocks, batching windows, and hardware memory all compete for the same resources.

Quantization is presented as a pipeline rather than a single switch: calibration, outlier handling, kernel support, and accuracy regression checks all matter.

The speaker highlights easy wins first: better batching, fewer copies, tighter tokenizers, and honest load tests before investing in exotic kernels.

A detailed section covers cache reuse, prefix sharing, and eviction policies, with guidance on when the complexity of a shared cache pays for itself.

Benchmarks are reported at the request level, with percentile latency, throughput under saturation, and memory headroom so that operators can reproduce the result.

items.abstract:

The session covers distributed training failure modes: stragglers, checkpoint storms, network contention, and silent numerical issues.

Regularization, replay data, and curriculum design are presented as tools for preserving general capability while specializing behavior.

The talk begins with data quality: deduplication, contamination checks, license review, and the long tail of formatting problems that break training runs.

Parameter-efficient methods are compared on memory, throughput, and the effort required to merge and serve adapters in production.

The speaker closes with a practical checklist for reproducible training runs, including environment pinning and artifact retention.

The speaker explains how to choose sequence length, packing strategy, and gradient accumulation so that the effective batch size matches the recipe.

The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment. items.title: Memory Architectures Compared
items.abstract:

The speaker closes with guidance on building retrieval APIs that agents can call repeatedly without flooding context windows.

The speaker demonstrates why embedding model changes require full reindexing and how to stage such migrations without breaking production.

Index design is covered in depth, including chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search, and reranking under tight latency budgets.

The session compares vector stores, inverted indexes, graph stores, and relational databases, arguing that the query pattern should choose the store.

The talk separates retrieval quality from memory quality: one is about finding evidence, the other about deciding what to keep and when to forget.

Several failure cases show retrieval systems confidently returning stale or contradictory evidence when freshness signals are missing.
